extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics and mathematical physicists (conference participants/readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Conference-length historical survey articles on early-20th-century mathematics and mathematical physics (reception of major ideas, biographies, conceptual transitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expectation for Minkowski's electrodynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Any reviewer of Minkowski’s electrodynamics had to either rewrite his equations in a recognizable form, or provide a precis of his formalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Einstein and Laub chose to rewrite Minkowski's equations in the usual three-dimensional form. When evaluating or presenting a novel formalism, explicitly map it to familiar notation or give a clear precis so readers can assess empirical/content claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coupling novel formalism to controversial physical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Minkowski committed a serious tactical error by coupling his four-dimensional formalism to a controversial electrodynamics of moving media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for authors: when introducing a novel mathematical/formal framework, avoid tying it too tightly to a controversial empirical theory; this can distract attention from the formal innovation and invite targeted criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacetime diagram as explanatory tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The spacetime diagram provides a comprehensible graphic illustration of the kinematics of the Lorentz group and the limit relation between pre-relativist and relativist mechanics (e.g., as c → ∞ axes collapse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spacetime diagrams to make unintuitive relativistic effects (Lorentz contraction, time dilation) appear as direct geometric consequences. Note representational artifacts (e.g., oblique axes are an artifact of the drawing though orthogonal in Minkowski geometry) and connections to earlier devices (Poincaré’s light ellipsoid corresponds to a projection of a light sphere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis on Erlangen Program: limited relation to Lie's theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Erlangen Program' had relatively little to do with Lie’s theory of continuous groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing Klein's program, emphasize its original concerns (projective/invariant theory) rather than reading it primarily as an early expression of Lie-group theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis on Erlangen Program: emphasis on invariant theory over group investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: It had less to do with the investigation of groups than with the systematic study of the invariant theory of well-known transformation groups (subgroups of the projective group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the Erlangen Program as an organizing principle focused on invariants of transformation groups (particularly projective-subgroups), not as a program whose central aim was group theory per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis on Erlangen Program: centrality of the Hauptgruppe (Euclidean transformations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hauptgruppe of Euclidean transformations was and remained of central importance for Klein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of Klein's work should account for the continued centrality he accorded Euclidean-transformation groups in applications and expositions (e.g., connections to mechanics and non-Euclidean geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis on Erlangen Program: tie to Klein's physicalist motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Erlangen Program' was tied to his physicalist motivation, an aspect of this story that became most evident after 1890.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical interpretation should consider Klein's physicalist concerns (links to mechanics, physics) as a driving motivation, not just abstract mathematical aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception phases of the Erlangen Program (three-phase schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three phases of reception: (1) initial phase where few read/understood the 1872 text and its content reflects Klein & Lie's research interests; (2) re-emergence in the 1890s via translations, Italian connections, and tension with Lie as Lie/Killing work attracted interest; (3) later phase (post-1890/into 1916) where Klein promoted the program in mechanics and relativity and integrated it into broader mathematical activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a phased account to analyze how a mathematical program's influence can be delayed, reinterpreted, and integrated across different communities (e.g., geometry, mechanics, relativity). Pay attention to translation, personal networks, and disciplinary shifts that trigger reappraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weyl feature (i): local vs. infinitesimal comparison; Weylian metric as (g, φ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct comparison of metrical quantities is possible only at the same point p by a Riemannian (or Lorentzian) metric g up to conformal rescaling; comparison between infinitesimally close points is achieved by a differential 1-form (scale/length connection) φ; a Weylian metric is given by the pair (g, φ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing Weyl's 1918 proposal, stress the two-part data (metric up to conformal factor and a scale connection) and the distinction between pointwise calibration and infinitesimal transfer (path-dependent scale transfer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weyl feature (ii): gauge symmetry and equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: A rescaling g → Ω^2 g (gauge symmetry) is accompanied by φ → φ − d log Ω; a Weylian metric is given (locally) by an equivalence class of pairs (g, φ) under these gauge transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Weyl metrics as gauge equivalence classes and explicate the transformation law for the scale connection when the metric is rescaled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weyl feature (iii): compatible affine connection and gauge-invariant curvatures
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a uniquely determined compatible affine connection Γ (Weyl geometric Levi-Civita connection) depending on φ but gauge invariant; derived curvature quantities (Riemann, Ricci, scalar) similarly have gauge-invariant status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight that despite gauge-dependent metric pieces, the connection and curvature constructions are well-defined and form the basis for geometric/physical deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weyl feature (iv): φ interpreted as electromagnetic potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Weyl interpreted the connection φ physically as the potential of an electromagnetic field and its curvature dφ as the electromagnetic field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note Weyl's physical identification linking geometry (scale connection) to electromagnetism — a central move in his attempt at geometric unification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weyl feature (v): gauge symmetry implies charge conservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gauge symmetry implies conservation of some current, here electrical charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing conceptual/physical consequences, record the inferred conservation law associated with Weyl gauge symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weyl feature (vi): scale connection linked to gravity (geometrical unification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scale connection was linked to gravity: geometrically unified field theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame Weyl's program as an attempt to geometrically unify gravity and electromagnetism by making scale structure dynamical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weyl feature (vii): enrichment of the Mie-Hilbert program
rubrics_metrics.description: Weyl's proposal enriched the Mie-Hilbert program (classical field theory of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate Weyl's work in the broader early-20th-century attempts to formulate classical unified field theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weyl feature (viii): lack of immediate empirical interpretation for g; calibration distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: No immediate empirical interpretation of the Riemannian component g was possible; Weyl proposed to distinguish calibration by adjustment and calibration by transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Weyl's physical plausibility, note the epistemic problem of interpreting the metric component and his proposed conceptual distinctions for calibration procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weyl feature (ix): Einstein's counter-argument from spectral stability (dφ ≠ 0 problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-vanishing curvature of the scale connection (dφ ≠ 0) leads to a puzzling behavior — Einstein's central counter-argument that it would produce unstable spectral lines of atomic oscillators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include Einstein's empirical objection when assessing the empirical viability of Weyl's original theory; this objection motivated later shifts from scale to phase gauge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Migration histories: Physics main line (I) with sub-stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics main line (ca. 1920–ca. 1980): (a) input to early unified field theories (1920s) then fading in 1930s; (b) migration to quantum mechanics with a shift from scale to phase gauge (1922–1929); (c) generalization to non-abelian symmetry groups in the 1950s; (d) eventual incorporation into the semiclassical core of the Standard Model between late 1960s–early 1980s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sequence to evaluate conceptual migration: how a geometric idea first proposed in classical gravity/electrodynamics settings transformed through quantum theory and gauge-field developments into modern particle-physics structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Migration histories: Foundations of differential geometry line (II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundations of differential geometry (ca. 1920–ca. 1960): (a) Weyl's and Cartan's analyses of the 'problem of space' supported Weyl's scale geometry as a foundational option and later led into the study of G-structures; (b) input to the conceptual/tool arsenal for general connections supplementing Cartan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing mathematical influence, track how Weyl's ideas fed into foundational debates and technical developments in differential geometry (connections, G-structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Migration histories: Reappearance of scale gauge (III) in late 20th century
rubrics_metrics.description: Reappearance (last third of the 20th century): restricted/integrable Weyl geometries regained interest in contexts such as (a) foundations of general relativity, (b) long-range forces and cosmology, (c) short-range forces/deep inelastic scattering, (d) connections with Bohmian QM, (e) scale-covariant semiclassical theories for mass generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this entry to assess modern revivals of historical ideas: identify contexts, specify whether revivals are full restorations or restricted/modified uses (e.g., integrable scale connections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three phases in Minkowski's development of convex bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 1 (∼1887–early work): Minkowski addressed the minimum problem for positive definite quadratic forms via a geometric/lattice method. Phase 2 (about 1891): he reframed lattices and associated bodies as objects prompting new questions, introducing notions like radial distance and 'Eichkörper', turning lattices into both objects and tools. Phase 3 (post-1897): Minkowski introduced the convex body as a defined geometric object investigated for its own sake (definition in 1897 paper), initiating systematic study of convex bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing conceptual emergence, use this three-phase schema: (1) methodological innovation applied to a known problem, (2) abstraction of method-objects into objects-of-study, (3) formal definition and autonomous research program. Cite the 1897 definition and subsequent papers/collected works as evidence of phase 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry-of-numbers method for the minimum problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Minkowski's geometric approach: associate a positive-definite quadratic form with an n-dimensional lattice (points with integer coordinates), place n-dimensional spheres with the smallest lattice distance as diameter around each lattice point, compare sphere volumes to the standard parallelotope volume to deduce bounds on the minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes a concrete methodological criterion for transforming number-theoretic minima problems into geometric volume comparisons; use it as a model for 'geometrization' of arithmetic problems and as an exemplar when evaluating similar arguments.
